1:
Job answers the charge that his longing for death is a crime by appealing first to the common condition of every man, asking whether there is not an appointed time to man upon earth. The reformed John Gill fixes the sense on the fixed bounds of a life: there is a set time for man's coming into the world, for his continuance in it, and for his going out of it, a term whose limits cannot be passed; and this belongs to man on earth, not to the eternity that awaits him in heaven or in hell, for his days here are but a shadow, and he returns to the earth at the appointed hour. The very word Enosh, Gill notes, bespeaks a frail, feeble, mortal creature, so that the name itself argues the shortness of the span.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same clause but catches in it the ring of a soldier's term of service: "Is there not a warfare (so the word is) to man upon earth?" Man's present place is the earth God has given to the children of men (Ps. 115:16), which bespeaks at once his meanness and God's mercy, that he is yet upon the earth and not under it, on earth and not in hell. His continuance here is for a time appointed by him that made us and set us here, so that we are governed not by the blind fortune of the Epicureans but by the wise and sovereign counsel of God; and during that time man's life is a warfare and as the days of a hireling, a soldier exposed to hardship among enemies, a day-labourer with the work of the day to do in its day and his account to make up at night.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the martial rendering further. Adam Clarke lays the Hebrew bare, halo tsaba leenosh aley arets, "Is there not a warfare to miserable man upon the earth?" and gathers the versions, the Septuagint's "place of trial" and the Vulgate's militia est vita hominis, to draw his own sense: human life is a state of probation, every day and place a time and place of exercise to train us up for eternal life. John Wesley keeps closer to Gill, hearing a time limited by God wherein man must live in this sinful and miserable world, and asking whether it be a crime to desire that God would bring him to that joyful period. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch settle the philology between them: tsaba is not the service of a labourer in the field but active military service, and then fatigue and toil in general, so that the verse likens life itself to a hard campaign whose only discharge is death.
2:
The comparison Job reaches for is the hireling's yearning at the end of a scorching day, when "a servant earnestly desireth the shadow" and the labourer waits for his wages. The reformed John Gill hears in that "shadow" two possible longings: either the shade of some great rock, tree, or hedge that would shelter the servant from the midday sun, so burdensome in those eastern countries, or the lengthening shadow of the evening and the setting sun, when the day's work is ended and the labourer retires to rest and refreshment. Since such a shadow, in either sense, is naturally and lawfully desired, Job argues, it ought not to be charged as a crime in him that he should as earnestly wish for the shadow of death, or the coming on of his long night.

The wesleyan-arminian voices settle on the evening. Adam Clarke pictures the man who labours hard in the heat and earnestly desires the long evening shadows, that he may rest from his toil, receive his day's wages, and go to his rest; and he takes the "shadow" for night itself, quoting Virgil and the grammarian Servius, that "night is the shadow of the earth." John Wesley reduces it to a phrase: the shadow is the sunset, the time allotted for the servant's rest.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the feeling of the image without pressing its botany. As a poor servant or hireling tired with his work wishes for the shadows of the evening, when he shall receive his penny and go to rest, so Job had, he thought, as much reason to wish for death. The darkness of night is as welcome to the labourer as the light of morning is to the watchman; the God of nature has provided for the repose of the weary, and no wonder they desire it. "The sleep of the labouring man is sweet," Henry adds from the Preacher, and no rich man takes so much satisfaction in his rent-days as the hireling in his day's wages.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch bind the simile to its intended point: like a servant who longs for the shade, and like a hireling who waits for his wages, so Job waits for death as refreshment and rest after hard labour. Yet they mark that he does not quite reach that consoling conclusion but remains on this side of it, for the rest he pants after is not yet come. Together the witnesses divide only mildly, over whether the coveted shadow is the noonday shelter or the shadow of nightfall, but they agree that the longing is honest, the longing of a spent man for the one relief his day still owes him, and that it is no more sinful in Job to wish for his grave than in the hireling to wish for his evening.
3:
The likeness turns bitter as Job applies it to himself: where the servant's evening brings wages and the labourer's night brings rest, his own reward is only that he is "made to possess months of vanity," and wearisome nights are appointed to him. The reformed John Gill is careful that the "so" of the verse does not tidily answer the similes before it, for Job's lot is the reverse of the hireling's, no refreshing shadow but months of emptiness, no rest but continual tossing. The time of his affliction, though in truth not long, seemed long enough to be reckoned in months, and some months had indeed passed since his calamities began; the very measure of months, Gill observes, tells how the days had dragged.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds the sting of the "vanity" not chiefly in pain but in uselessness. Job was wholly taken off from business and unfit for it; every day was a burden because he was in no capacity of doing good or of spending it to any purpose. He calls these "months of vanity," and Henry marks that Job insists not so much that they are days in which he has no pleasure as that they are days in which he does no good, and on that account they are months of vanity. It much increases the affliction of sickness and age to a good man, Henry adds, that he is thereby forced from his usefulness; yet when we are disabled to work for God, if we will but sit still quietly for him, it is all one, and we shall be accepted.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch sharpen the word itself. What the older English renders "vanity" they take in its primary force of nothingness, error, and disappointment, the same sense the term carries elsewhere in the book, so that these are "months of disappointment," months that one after another cheat the hope of the sick man of his longed-for recovery. It is by this, they suggest, that we are to imagine the friends' comfort mocked, each month promising relief and every one delivering none.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the sufferer's experience: the night, which for others relieves the toil of the day, is no relief to Job but only a continuance of his anxiety and labour. He is like the hireling with his appointed task still before him, and like the soldier harassed by the enemy, obliged to be continually on the watch, always on the look-out, with scarcely any rest. The witnesses do not divide over the misery; they differ only in accent, Gill and Henry on the emptiness of days that do no good, Keil and Delitzsch on the recurring disappointment of a hope deferred, and Clarke on the ceaseless watch that turns even the night into labour.
4:
The wearisome nights of the last verse are now heard from within, in the sick man's own broken cry: no sooner does he lie down than he asks, "When shall I arise?" and the night stretches out with tossings to and fro until the dawn. The reformed John Gill catches the restlessness of it: as soon as Job composed himself to sleep, hoping for the refreshment his bed should give, he said within himself, or aloud to those who watched with him, "Oh that it were time to rise!" For the bed that should have eased him only wearied him more and lengthened his sense of the night.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the picture of a man whom continual affliction allows no respite. He has so little rest that when he does lie down he longs for the returning light that he may rise, and he can find ease in no posture, continually shifting his place in the bed and finding relief nowhere, "full of tossings," as Job himself says. Nothing, Clarke reflects, could better depict the state of a man under continual afflictions which afford him no respite, his days and his nights alike spent in constant anguish.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the couplet to bring out its weariness: "When I lie down, then I say, When shall I arise? But the night is long, and I am filled with tossings to and fro till the morning twilight." The night, measured by a sleepless man, has no end but the slow greying of the dawn.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the loss in its full pathos. The night relieves the toil of the day, he says, not only for labourers but for sufferers; if a sick man can but get a little sleep, it helps nature, and it is hoped he will do well. Whatever the trouble, sleep gives some intermission to the cares and pains and griefs that afflict us; it is "the parenthesis of our sorrows." But poor Job could gain no such relief. His nights were wearisome, and instead of taking any rest he did but tire himself the more with tossing to and fro until morning. Those in great uneasiness, through pain of body or anguish of mind, think by changing sides, changing places, and changing postures to get some ease; but while the cause is the same within, it is all to no purpose, a very resemblance, Henry says, of a fretful, discontented spirit that is ever shifting and never easy. So the night that others bless as their rest became the thing Job most dreaded, and he lay down only to ask when it would be gone. The witnesses do not divide; they gather one portrait of a man for whom the appointed hours of repose had themselves become a torment.
5:
From his sleepless bed the complaint descends to the body itself, whose "flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust," its skin broken and grown loathsome. The reformed John Gill takes the words not of the grave, as some would, but of Job's present misery: his ulcers bred worms or vermin that spread over his body, the scabs of his disease crusting upon him like a garment; and as he sat and rolled himself in dust and ashes, the running matter of his sores mingled with the dust and clotted into clods that covered him, a dismal spectacle, Gill says, a precious saint in a vile body.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same horror as a lesson: his sores bred worms, the scabs were like clods of dust, and his skin was broken, so evil was the disease that cleaved fast to him. See, Henry urges, what vile bodies we have, and how little reason to pamper them or be proud of them, since they carry in themselves the seeds of their own corruption; as fond as we now are of them, the time may come when we loathe them and long to be rid of them.

Here the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke breaks with the older expositors over the "clods of dust." The worms he takes literally enough, for the ulcerated flesh, open to the air, would attract the insects that deposit their eggs in such places; but the clods, he thinks, all the commentators have missed. They are the incrustations of dried matter that form on decaying sores, the furfuraceous scales that fall continually from the body in the elephantiasis, when the skin grows so rigid that it cracks across at the joints and exudes a loathsome ichor. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the disease the same way: it is characteristic of elephantiasis that the skin becomes hard and rugous, and then cracks and becomes ulcerated, which is the "skin broken and become loathsome" of the verse.

The other witnesses hold to the plainer picture. John Wesley, another wesleyan-arminian voice, glosses simply that the worms were bred out of Job's corrupted flesh and sores, the dust was the dust of the earth on which he lay, and the skin was broken by ulcers in every part of it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the received rendering, the flesh clothed with worms and clods of dust and the skin broken and become loathsome, as the sober record of a body wasting under a real and nameable disease. So the division is genuine but narrow: whether the "clods of dust" are literal earth caked upon the sores by dust and ashes, as Gill and Wesley take it, or the hard scales and crusts of the elephantiasis itself, as Clarke and Ellicott insist.
6:
Turning from his ruined body to his dwindling time, Job cries that his days "are swifter than a weaver's shuttle," and are spent without hope. The reformed John Gill weighs which days are meant: not his days of affliction, which in his apprehension crept slowly and which he could have wished to pass faster, but his days in common, and especially his days of prosperity and pleasure, which were soon over and which he sometimes wished back again. The shuttle, thrown swiftly to and fro across the web, is one of several biblical figures for the speed of a fleeting life.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke stops over the very word. The Hebrew areg, he argues, signifies rather the weaver than his shuttle, and he even doubts whether the shuttle was in use in Job's day; yet some such instrument must have been in view, or the figure loses its force. In almost every nation, he observes, human life has been compared to a web and its span to a thread woven through it, whence arose the fable of the three Fates, one holding the distaff, one spinning the thread, and one cutting it off when life must end. Job represents his own thread as spun out with great rapidity and about to be cut; and "spent without hope" means that expectation of future good was at an end, for where the hope of relief is gone, there is despair. Clarke sets beside the verse the same image from the prophet, "my life is cut off, as by the weaver" (Isa. 38:12), and Coverdale's homely rendering, that our days "passe over more spedely then a weaver can weave out his webbe."

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the common image and its double point: the shuttle passes in a moment from one end of the web to the other, and so the time of Job's life hastens to its period; "without hope" he takes of the hope of enjoying any good day here below.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the shuttle into a meditation. Time hastens on apace, its motion cannot be stopped, and once past it cannot be recalled; every day, like the shuttle, leaves a thread behind it, and while we live we are, as we sow (Gal. 6:8), so also weaving. Many weave the spider's web, which will fail them (ch. 8:14); but if we are weaving for ourselves the holy garments and robes of righteousness, we shall have the benefit of them when our work comes to be reviewed, and every man shall reap as he sowed and wear as he wove. The witnesses do not divide over the sense of the flying shuttle, only over its grammar, whether the word names the weaver or the tool, but they agree that the thread of Job's life seemed to him all but run out, and, as he thought, run out without hope.
7:
"O remember that my life is wind" — and with that sigh Job turns from his friends to God himself, pleading his own frailty as the ground of pity. The reformed John Gill reads it as a direct address to God: man's life is in his breath, and that breath in his nostrils, a thing not to be depended on; it is a vapour, an air-bubble, easily broken, and, like the wind, full of stir and noise yet swiftly passing and not returning. God cannot forget, Gill grants, nor needs to be reminded of anything; but he may seem to forget the frailty of man when he lays his hand heavy upon him, and to remember it when he mercifully takes the hand away, and this remembering is what Job here begs.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears a dying man commending himself to God's compassion as a weak and fleeting creature, whose abode is short, whose removal is sure, and whose return is impossible. His life is wind, as the lives of all men are, noisy perhaps and blustering, but empty, soon gone, and, once gone, past recall; God had compassion on Israel, Henry recalls, remembering that they were but flesh, "a wind that passeth away and cometh not again" (Ps. 78:39). Such plain truths of the shortness and vanity of life do us good, he says, when we think of them with application to ourselves: we must shortly close the eye of the body and "no more see good," the good that most men set their hearts on (Ps. 4:6); let us therefore live by the faith which is the evidence of things not seen.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke records another turn of the verse. Mr. Good would render it, "O remember that, if my life pass away, mine eye shall turn no more to scenes of goodness," that is, never again shall Job witness those tokens of divine favour that till now had been so perpetually his; yet Clarke judges that the common translation, "my life is wind," gives a very good sense of its own.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the reach of the words: "Remember that my life is a breath, that my eye will never again look on prosperity." We see good, they explain, that is, prosperity and joy, only in the present life; with death it ends. So the appeal is not merely to God's mercy but to the brevity of the only span in which mercy, as Job now conceives it, can still be shown him. The witnesses do not divide; they gather around one plea, that the God who has laid so heavy a hand should remember how little of the man is left for it to fall upon.
8:
Job presses the thought of his vanishing further: soon "the eye of him that hath seen me shall see me no more," and even God's own eye, turned to seek him, will find him gone. The reformed John Gill takes the first clause of the sharpest, quickest eye, which after death shall not reach him, with the qualification that the dead are still seen of the omniscient God, and the souls of the godly are at once present with him and beheld by angels and by glorified saints; the meaning is that once a man is dead he is seen no more among the living.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the removal to an unseen world. The eye of him that has seen Job here shall see him no more there, for it is a state unseen; death removes our friends into darkness and will shortly remove us out of their sight, so that when we go hence we shall be seen no more, but go to converse with the things that are eternal (Ps. 39:13). And God can do it in a moment: "Thine eyes are upon me, and I am not," for God can look him into eternity and frown him into the grave whenever he pleases.

The witnesses divide, gently, over that haunting last clause. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke offers two turns of it: "Thou canst look me into nothing," or else, "Let thine eye be upon me as one judged to death, and I shall immediately cease to live among men." John Wesley reads it the first way, "if thou cast one angry look upon me, I am not; thou canst look me into eternity." But the grammatical-historical witnesses take the eyes to be seeking, not slaying. Charles Ellicott renders it "thine own eyes shall look for me, but I shall be no more," appealing to the Septuagint and the Vulgate; and Keil and Delitzsch give the same, "Thine eyes look for me, and I am no more," a picture not of a look that annihilates but of a God who turns to find his creature and finds the place empty.

Clarke adds the pathos that gives the verse its edge: should Job die now, under all this load of undeserved odium his friends have heaped on him, he would never have opportunity to vindicate his character or regain the good opinion of mankind, and the grave would close over him with the wrong still upon him. The witnesses do not finally quarrel; they only weigh whether the divine eye in the second line destroys or searches, and either way they leave Job the same, here a moment, and then, under that eye, gone.
9:
"As the cloud is consumed and vanisheth away" — Job takes the summer cloud for his emblem, so that he who goeth down to the grave comes up no more. The reformed John Gill notes that a cloud, once dispersed by the wind or broken up by the sun, is never seen again; and though the wise man speaks of clouds returning after the rain, those are not the same clouds but new ones succeeding. The same figure, Gill observes, serves elsewhere for the blotting out of pardoned sin, that it may be no more seen or remembered; but here the point is less the suddenness of life's passing than its irrevocableness once it is gone, as the application in the next verses shows.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott prizes the aptness of the image: it is a fine simile that man is as evanescent as a cloud, "and very apt, because, whether it vanishes on the surface of the sky or is distributed in rain, nothing more completely passes away than the summer cloud." It is an appearance only, which comes to nought; and such, Job would say, is man.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the comparison the same way: as the cloud is dissipated, so is the breath of those that go down to the grave; as that cloud shall never return, so the dead return no more to sojourn among the living. John Wesley guards the phrase "no more" with the one exception faith requires, that it is no more "until the general resurrection"; and he turns the sight of a vanishing cloud into a sermon: when we see a cloud that looked great, as if it would eclipse the sun, of a sudden dispersed and gone, let us say, Just such a thing is the life of man, a vapour that appears for a while and then vanisheth away.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the lesson without softening its warning. Dying is a work to be done but once, and therefore it had need be well done, for an error there is past retrieve; the scattering of a cloud illustrates it, for the cloud is consumed and vanishes, resolved into air and never knit again. Other clouds arise, but the same cloud never returns; so a new generation of the children of men is raised up, but the former is quite consumed and passes away. It concerns us, Henry concludes, to secure a better place when we die. The witnesses do not divide; they let the summer cloud say for them what Job means, that the life which melts into the sky does not gather itself again, and that the grave, in the order of this world, gives none of its own back.
10:
The cloud's law is now applied to the man's own door: "he shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more." The reformed John Gill reads the "house" in more senses than one, literally the dwelling he built or hired, to which a good man will have no wish to return, having a better house eternal in the heavens; or figuratively his body, the earthly house of his tabernacle, to which he shall not come back until the resurrection rebuilds it; or his family and household affairs, in which he shall bear no more part, as David said of his dead child, "I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is careful that the verse be not made to prove too much. Its language is echoed in the Psalter, "his place shall know him no more" (Ps. 103:16), and we need not force the words as though they forbade ascribing to Job any belief in a future life or a resurrection; for under any construction they are simply and accurately true of man as we know him here. Even if he live again in another way, it is not in this world that he lives again, and it is of this world and of man in this world that Job is speaking. Man in the aspect of his mortality is truly a pitiable object, demanding our compassion; and, Ellicott adds, the appeal to man's Maker is not in vain, for He who made him what he is has looked upon his misery.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke guards the same ground: Job does not mean that he shall be annihilated, but that he shall never more become an inhabitant of the earth. The word rendered "grave," he notes, may signify the state of the dead, or any deep pit, and here the sense is simply that the man returns no more to his former place. John Wesley presses the practical edge, that Job shall no more be seen or known in his former habitation, and "it concerns us to secure a better place when we die, for this will own us no more."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry rounds the thought to its solemn breadth: others will take possession and keep the house till they too resign it to another generation. Glorified saints shall return no more to the cares and burdens and sorrows of their house, nor damned sinners to its gaieties and pleasures; their place shall no more know them, own them, or be under their influence. It concerns us, Henry says with Wesley, to secure a better place when we die, for this one will no more acknowledge us. The witnesses do not divide; and where a reader might fear the verse denied a life to come, Ellicott and Clarke expressly keep the door open, for Job speaks of return to this world, and of that alone.
11:
From the certainty of a death that gives nothing back, Job draws his resolve: "therefore I will not refrain my mouth," but will speak in the anguish of his spirit and complain in the bitterness of his soul. The reformed John Gill sets out the reasoning: beyond the common lot of a life that is warfare and sorrow, extraordinary afflictions had been laid upon Job that made life insupportable; he saw no good in the present, expected none in the grave, and would return to enjoy none, and therefore he would not be silent. Gill records Jarchi's turn of the "also" in the Hebrew as a kind of just retaliation: since God will not refrain his hand from Job, Job will not refrain his mouth from God; since no mercy is shown, he will utter his miserable complaint aloud. Yet Gill will not excuse it, for this was Job's infirmity, where he should rather have held his peace like Aaron, been dumb like David, and owned the sovereignty of God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the resolve against a better example. From the same premises of life's frailty, holy David had made the contrary use, "I was dumb, I opened not my mouth" (Ps. 39:9); but Job, finding himself near expiring, hastens to make his complaint as if he could not die in peace until he had given vent to his passion. When we have but a few breaths to draw, Henry counsels, we should spend them in the holy, gracious breathings of faith and prayer, not in the noisome, noxious breathings of sin and corruption; better to die praying and praising than complaining and quarrelling.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the resolve more gently. Adam Clarke states it plainly, that all is hopeless, and Job will therefore indulge his complaint. John Wesley draws out the sufferer's own logic: since his life is so vain and short, and once lost is past all recovery, he will plead with God for pity before he dies; he will not smother his anguish within his breast, but will ease himself by pouring out his complaint. So the witnesses circle a genuine question of judgment without wholly settling it, whether Job's refusal to keep silence was a pardonable easing of an overburdened heart, as Clarke and Wesley incline to hear it, or the infirmity of a good man who forgot for a moment to be still under the hand of God, as Gill and Henry more soberly judge. What none of them denies is that the words are wrung from real anguish, and that the mouth Job would not refrain speaks the bitterness of a soul at the end of its strength.
12:
"Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me?" — Job protests that he is treated as though he were some vast and dangerous power needing to be penned and guarded. The reformed John Gill runs through the images the words might carry: is he like the restless sea that casts up mire and dirt, or the raging sea whose proud waves must be curbed, or a wild sea-monster, the leviathan, the crooked serpent, an emblem of cruel princes and tyrants? He was, Gill answers, the very reverse of all this, gentle to the poor and distressed in his prosperity, no oppressor to be restrained, and yet he is hedged and watched as if he were.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports the Targum's reading, which asks whether Job is condemned like the Egyptians drowned in the Red Sea, or like Pharaoh, that a keeper should be set over him; but Clarke judges the common version less exceptionable and the meaning plain enough. Job is hedged about and shut in with insuperable difficulties, entangled like a wild beast in a net, so that the more he struggles the more his strength is lost. As God set the sand for the bound of the sea by a perpetual decree (Jer. 5:22), and shut up the sea with doors and bars, saying "hitherto shalt thou come, but no further" (ch. 38:11), so Job feels his afflictions to be the very bars and keepers set to hold him in, as though he were as dangerous as the sea, ready to overwhelm the earth.

The grammatical-historical witnesses find the same background. Charles Ellicott explains the hard verse from Scripture itself, and thinks the writer, likely familiar with Egypt, had in view the Nile, still called "the sea," carefully watched and guarded by dykes lest its overflow destroy the land; so Job cries, Am I the sea, or one of its monsters, that Thou keepest guard over me and shuttest me up so fast that I cannot get free? Keil and Delitzsch render it "Am I a sea, or a sea-monster, that thou settest a watch over me?" and note that a watch upon the sea can only be designed to hold its swelling within bounds, which is precisely the indignity Job feels.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the lesson the complaint half conceals: we are very apt in affliction to complain of God as if he laid more restraint upon us than there is occasion for, keeping us in as though we were some raging sea or unruly monster that needed all these mighty bonds. Whereas, Henry answers, we are never in heaviness but when there is need, nor more than the necessity demands. So the witnesses converge: the figure is one of a power under guard, whether the drowned Egyptians of the Targum or the bounded sea of Jeremiah and Job, and its sting is Job's sense that God watches him as an enemy too strong to be left free, a sense the witnesses honour as real yet gently correct.
13:
Job traces his misery back to the very place where men look for rest, telling how he had promised himself that "my bed shall comfort me, my couch shall ease my complaint." The reformed John Gill reads it as the sick man's reasonable hope: thinking within himself that he would lie down and try to get a little sleep, which might comfort and refresh him, Job counted on the relief he had known in better days from an ordinary night's rest. The bed is where the weary promise themselves ease; Job promised it to himself, and the promise failed.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch gather the whole movement of which this is the opening, the bed that should comfort, the couch that should help him bear his complaint, and then the dreams and visions by which that hope is overthrown. They render the couplet closely: when he says his bed shall comfort him and his couch ease his complaint, then he is scared with dreams and terrified through visions, so that his soul chooses strangling and death rather than his wasted frame. The verse sets up the cruel reversal by which the appointed place of rest becomes the scene of a fresh terror.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the disappointed expectation with a pastor's tenderness. There, he says, we promise ourselves some repose when we are fatigued with labour or pain: "my bed shall comfort me, and my couch shall ease my complaint"; sleep will for a time give some relief, for it is appointed to that end, and many a time it has eased us so that we awake refreshed and with new vigour. When it is so, Henry adds, we have great reason to be thankful. But it was not so with poor Job. His bed, instead of comforting him, terrified him; his couch, instead of easing his complaint, added to it, and it was this that made the night so unwelcome and wearisome to him, so that he asked, as the earlier verse recorded, "When shall I arise?" (v.4). Henry draws the sobering note that God can, when he pleases, meet us with terror even where we promise ourselves ease and repose, and make us a terror to ourselves; that which has often been our refreshment he can turn into our punishment. The witnesses do not divide; they let the verse stand as the hinge of Job's night, the settled human expectation that the bed will comfort, spoken just before it is shattered, and they feel with him the peculiar cruelty of a rest that betrays the man who lies down to take it.
14:
The rest Job hoped for turns to horror, for "then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions." The reformed John Gill traces the sources of these night-terrors. They were not dreams told him by another, as Eliphaz had his vision, but dreams Job himself dreamed, arising perhaps from the force of his distemper and the pain that broke his sleep and set his fancy roving upon dreadful objects; or from the melancholy his afflictions had bred; or from Satan, into whose hand he had been given and who was permitted to disturb him. All of these Job ascribes to God, Gill notes, because God suffered it so to be; and thus the very dreams, instead of refreshing him, added to his sufferings, so that he was the worse and not the better for his bed and his couch.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke has no doubt of the agent behind the images. Satan was permitted to haunt Job's imagination with dreadful dreams and terrific appearances, so that as soon as he fell asleep he was suddenly roused and alarmed by these appalling shapes. He needed the rest that sleep should give, yet was afraid to close his eyes because of the horrid images that would rise before his imagination; and Clarke asks whether a state more deplorable than this could be conceived.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the couplet in its place in the sequence, rendering it "Then thou scaredst me with dreams, and didst wake me up in terror from visions," the visions of the night not soothing but startling the sufferer out of what little sleep he had. The dream that should have been the parenthesis of his sorrows becomes another instrument of them.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds together the two hands at work in these terrors. Job's dreams might partly arise from his distemper, for in fevers and sore diseases the sleep is commonly unquiet; yet Henry thinks Satan also had a hand, for he delights to terrify those whom it is out of his reach to destroy. Job, however, looked up to God, who permitted it, "thou scarest me," and took Satan's frightful representations for the very terrors of God setting themselves in array against him. Henry turns it to prayer: we have reason to ask God that our dreams may neither defile nor disquiet us, that he who keeps Israel and neither slumbers nor sleeps may keep us when we slumber and sleep, so that the devil may do us no mischief as an insinuating serpent or a roaring lion, and to bless God when we lie down and our sleep is sweet and we are not thus scared. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the distemper opened the door, that Satan was the tormentor, and that God, who permitted all, is the one to whom Job, rightly or in his anguish, refers the whole.
15:
Driven past endurance, Job says his very soul now "chooseth strangling, and death rather than my life." The reformed John Gill is careful that this is no design of self-murder: not that Job would strangle himself, as Ahithophel did, nor be strangled by another as criminals were, but that he would welcome death in whatever shape it came, even a suffocating disease that stops the breath, so weary was he of life under his heavy afflictions. Death in any form, Gill says, is but the stopping of a man's breath, and it was death that Job chose, come how it might.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the choice a physical cause. In his broken and dismal slumbers Job likely felt an oppression and difficulty of breathing, something like the incubus or nightmare; and, distressing as that was, he would prefer even death by such suffocation to any longer life in such misery. The horror of the night bleeds into the wish for the grave.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fasten on the last word of the verse. Charles Ellicott renders it "my soul maketh choice of strangling and death rather than a life like this," but marks that the Hebrew reads literally "than my bones," or, as some take it, "a death by these my members," that is, a death inflicted by himself, suicide. Keil and Delitzsch turn the same phrase starkly, "So that my soul chose suffocation, death rather than this skeleton," the wasted frame that Job's body had become, which he would gladly exchange for the grave. The word that the older English softens into "my life" is, in the Hebrew, the very bones and members of the sufferer, so that he chooses death over the ruin his own body has become.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names the choice and will not gild it. Job's soul, his judgment as he thought, but really his passion, chose strangling and death rather than such a life as this, any death rather than this. This, Henry owns, was Job's infirmity; for though a good man would choose death rather than sin, as the martyrs did, and would not wish to live always in a world of temptation, yet he should be content to live as long as it pleases God, and not choose death rather than life, "because life is our opportunity of glorifying God and getting ready for heaven." So the witnesses agree on the desperate preference Job voices, while the grammatical readers press what exactly he weighs against death, whether "my life," or literally "my bones," the very skeleton he had become; and Henry alone steps back to mark that the choice, however understandable, was the sufferer's weakness and not his wisdom.
16:
"I loathe it; I would not live alway" — the words gather up the whole night's despair, though the witnesses differ over what it is that Job loathes and how the second clause should be read. The reformed John Gill offers more than one construction of "I loathe it": either Job loathes his life, which had become a weariness to him, or his very bones, so painful and nauseous; or the sense is "I am become loathsome," to himself, his servants, his friends, and even his wife; or again, being ulcerated, "I pine and waste away," and so must quickly be gone.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the loathing of life itself: in such circumstances life is hateful to him, and though men naturally wish for length of days, Job would, if long life were offered with the sufferings he now bore, despise the offer and spurn the boon. Clarke notes Mr. Good's bolder rendering of the surrounding lines, "No longer would I live! O, release me! How are my days vanity!" a cry to be let go rather than held in such an existence.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears the clause turn, at the last, toward comfort. "I loathe it," he takes of the thought of self-destruction, or of Job's life, though he allows the alternative "I waste away" as less probable; but on the famous second clause he parts from the older English. Rather than the Authorised Version's wish, "I would not live always," Ellicott finds a ray of comfort in the plain statement of fact, "I shall not live for ever," which he judges more in accordance with the context, not a petulant refusal of life, but the sick man's solace that his misery cannot last beyond his few days. Keil and Delitzsch render the whole line to the same weary effect, "I loathe it, I would not live alway; let me alone, for my days are breath," the days so few and so empty that Job asks only to be left in peace to the end of them.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the confession with his usual balance. Job was sick of life and hated the thought of it: "I would not live always," he says, and not only would he not live always in pain, but not always even in ease and prosperity, since a good man has a better world in prospect and would not, if he might, live always in a world of sin and temptation. Yet Henry marks the danger in it too, that Job's judgment was here overborne by his passion. So the witnesses divide, quietly, over the very grammar of despair, whether the line is a wish that recoils from life, as Henry and the older version take it, or a comfort that death will end the misery, "I shall not live for ever," as Ellicott hears it, and over what Job loathes, his life, his bones, or himself grown loathsome to all around him.
17:
"What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him?" — Job takes up the language of the psalmist's wonder, but bends it to a strange and bitter use, and the witnesses divide over whether the question breathes complaint or awe. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lays out both readings side by side. It may be a passionate reflection on the proceedings of divine justice, as if the great God demeaned himself in contending with so mean a creature: great men think it below them to take notice of their inferiors' follies, so why does God "magnify" man by visiting him, trying him, and pouring all his forces upon one so unequal a match, visiting him with afflictions that, like a quotidian ague, return as duly as the morning light? Or it may be a pious admiration of divine condescension, like the wonder of the eighth Psalm (Ps. 8:4) and the hundred and forty-fourth (Ps. 144:3): that God should put such honour upon poor, weak man as to take him into covenant and communion, set his heart upon him as one dear to him, visit him every morning as we visit a friend, and try him every moment as one jealous over him. That a worm of the earth should be the darling of heaven is matter for everlasting wonder.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses hear the two senses as well. Adam Clarke sets them out: either "man is not worth thy notice, why then dost thou contend with him?" or "how astonishing thy kindness, that thou shouldest fix thy heart on such a poor, base, impotent creature as man, and mark him with such particular notice of thy providence and grace!" and he gives Calmet's paraphrase, "O Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest concern thyself about me." John Wesley leans to the complaint: what is there in poor, mean, miserable man that should induce God to take such notice of him, to make so much account of him, man being not worthy of God's favour, and yet below his anger, that God should concern himself so much about him as one near and dear to him?

The reformed John Gill reads the marvel as grace: man in his best estate was but earthly and mutable, and in his fallen estate a frail, feeble, sinful creature, so that it is wonderful indeed that God should magnify any of the race, should set his heart upon them, choose them to grace here and glory hereafter, and, through the incarnation of his Son, espouse them to himself and share his glory with them. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the key to Job's strange turn: the questions are in some degree a parody of the eighth Psalm (Ps. 8:5), and of the mercies new every morning (Lam. 3:23). Where the psalmist marvels that God so exalts and crowns puny man, Job complains that, instead of ignoring him, God makes too much of him, selecting so perishable a creature to be the fixed object of his relentless attention. The witnesses do not resolve the question so much as hold it open: the same words that in David are the song of grateful wonder are in Job, at least half, the protest of a man who wishes God would look away.
18:
The wonder of the last verse runs on into this one, that God should "visit him every morning, and try him every moment," and here the witnesses part over whether the visiting is mercy or scrutiny. The reformed John Gill lays out both. Taken in love, God has visited man in raising up his Son to be a Redeemer, in calling men by his grace, and in renewing his mercies to them every morning, a visitation that is matter of admiration. But the word may be taken otherwise, for visiting in the way of chastisement, since to punish or to correct is also a "visiting"; and so understood, God visits his people every morning with the rod, as the sufferer feels. Gill lets the two senses stand together, the gracious visit and the correcting one, both true of the God who deals so closely with man.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the visiting, in Job's mouth, as the relentless return of affliction: God visits him with troubles that, like a daily ague, come back as duly and constantly as the morning light, and tries him every moment to see what he can bear. Yet even as he voices the complaint, Henry hears beneath it the truer note of the parallel psalms, that for God to visit man at all, to feel his pulse and observe his looks as in care over him, is a condescension no creature could claim. The complaint and the wonder lie folded together in the one word "visit."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read Job's questions as the dark underside of the psalmist's praise. Where the eighth Psalm rejoices that God is mindful of man and crowns him, Job turns it about: this ceaseless visiting every morning and trying every moment is not honour but a burden, the perpetual attention of a God who will not, even for the space of a breath, let his creature be. The trying, they note, is the testing of one held fast under an examining eye that never lifts.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley gathers the several strands. God visits man with mercy and blessing, so far honouring and regarding him as by his visitation to preserve his spirit and hold his soul in life; and he tries him, which God does not only by afflictions but also by prosperity, and by both inward and outward blessings, observing his motions every moment as in care for him and jealous over him. So the witnesses divide over the colour of the word rather than its fact: whether the morning visitation Job feels is the tender mercy new every day, as Gill's first sense and Wesley allow, or the daily-returning rod and the moment-by-moment testing under which Job groans, as Henry and Keil and Delitzsch hear it. What all agree is that the verse marvels, whether in gratitude or in grief, that the infinite God should stoop to so unremitting a dealing with so small a creature.
19:
The wonder curdles into a plea for a moment's respite: "how long wilt thou not depart from me, nor let me alone till I swallow down my spittle?" The reformed John Gill hears in "depart from me" a cry to be released from the wrestling and contending of God's afflicting hand, the Lord too strong a combatant for Job, who would rather be quit of the struggle. Following Broughton, Gill would even render it "how long wilt thou not look off from me?" not a look of love, which Job would never wish averted, but the frowning, angry look God had put on toward him; and he catches the metaphor of wrestlers who fix a sharp and constant gaze upon each other while they grapple, so that Job begs God to take off the eye that never leaves him.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "How long dost thou not look away from me, nor let me alone till I swallow down my spittle?" the same image of an examining gaze from which the sufferer pleads to be freed if only for an instant. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes that instant by the proverb Job uses: to "swallow down my spittle" is a saying still current among the Arabs, meaning the least imaginable space, "let me draw my breath, give me a moment, even the twinkling of an eye." Job is urged by his sufferings to keep up his complaint, but his strength is spent and his mouth dry, and he asks only for so short a pause as would let him moisten his parched tongue and speak again.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees that "till I swallow down my spittle" is doubtless a proverbial expression, like "the twinkling of an eye" or "while I fetch a breath." John Wesley, another wesleyan-arminian voice, reads it the same way, "how long will it be ere thou withdraw thy afflicting hand?" and "that I may have a breathing time," a proverbial phrase for the smallest respite.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry feels the weight of that image of a man who cannot so much as swallow. It should seem, he says, that Job's distemper lay much in his throat and almost choked him, so that he could not swallow his spittle; he complains elsewhere that it bound him like the collar of his coat (ch. 30:18). "Lord," Job in effect asks, "wilt thou not give me some respite, some breathing-time?" echoing his own plea that God would not take away the little breath he had (ch. 9:18). The witnesses do not divide; they gather one small, human petition out of the great complaint, that the God whose eye and hand are never off him would look away, even for the space of a swallowed breath, and give a tormented man one instant's peace.
20:
Job comes at last to the ground of it all, "I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men?" and the witnesses divide twice over, whether the words are a confession or a supposition, and whether the God addressed is the Preserver of men or their Watcher. The reformed John Gill takes the opening as a real acknowledgment, though not of the notorious crimes his friends charged: Job owns that he is a sinner, guilty of daily sin as the best of men are, and so no match for a holy God, unable to answer him for one fault of a thousand, and therefore he asks what he can do, and begs God to depart from him.

The grammatical-historical witnesses read the clause as concessive rather than contrite. Charles Ellicott renders it "putting the case that I have sinned, yet what then can I do unto Thee, O thou keeper of men?" with a possible glance back at the sea and its keeper in the verse before (v.12). Keil and Delitzsch agree that "I have sinned" is hypothetical, granted that I have sinned, what harm could I do to Thee, an inferential question and not an admission of the guilt his friends allege. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports Kennicott's bolder view, that the words are addressed to Eliphaz and not to God, "you say I must have been a sinner; what then? I have not sinned against thee, O thou spy upon mankind"; though Clarke gives also the reading that takes God as the hearer, "Be it that I have sinned, what injury can I do unto thee, O thou Observer of man?" John Wesley finds room for a genuine confession within the supposition: though free from the crying sins for which his friends suppose the judgment sent, Job freely owns himself a sinner, and therefore obnoxious to God's justice, with nothing to say or do if God should mark iniquities.

Beneath this runs the second division, over the title Job gives God. The word, some render "Preserver" or "Saviour of men," and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears it so, God the observer and preserver whose eye is upon man for good; on this reading Job's very complaint carries a seed of hope, that the God who keeps men will keep him. But Clarke's "spy upon mankind" and the common "Observer of men" turn the same word toward scrutiny, the watcher from whom nothing can be hidden. Henry draws the pastoral use: when we are convinced that we have sinned and brought it to owning, we cannot but conclude that something must be done to prevent its fatal consequence; and the enquiry "what shall I do unto thee?" is best made while we eye God as the Saviour and not the destroyer of men, "Thou art the Saviour of men; be my Saviour." The witnesses thus leave the verse poised between confession and protest, and between the God who watches to condemn and the God who preserves to save.
21:
"And why dost thou not pardon my transgression, and take away mine iniquity?" — the speech ends not in defiance but in a plea for pardon, urged by the nearness of the grave: "for now shall I sleep in the dust; and thou shalt seek me in the morning, but I shall not be." The reformed John Gill dwells on the word "pardon," which is literally to "lift up": every sin is a transgression whose guilt is a burden too heavy to bear, and pardon lifts it off, the Lord having lifted the sin from his people and laid it upon his Son, who bore it and took it away, so that when applied to the conscience it eases and removes it, as far as the east is from the west. For such a lifting Job here sues, with the God who has forgiveness with him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the prayer grow more earnest as the heat of Job's spirit, which made his complaints so bitter, makes his petition so lively. Job means more than the removal of his outward trouble; he is earnest for the return of God's favour, the want of which he had bewailed before (ch. 6:4). Where God pardons the transgression committed by us, Henry adds, his grace takes away the iniquity that reigns in us, for wherever he removes the guilt of sin he breaks its power. And Job enforces the prayer with the prospect of a quick death: he had complained of restless nights, but those who cannot sleep on a bed of down shall shortly sleep in a bed of dust, and "thou shalt seek me in the morning, to show me favour, but I shall not be"; if his sins are not pardoned while he lives, it will be too late.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the plea "after the manner of men": if God has any design to save Job, why not pardon him now, while he is a dying man, seeing that tomorrow God may seek him to do him good and find him gone? And Clarke insists that Job does not here criminate himself, as the older English might suggest, for he has repeatedly asserted his innocence, and Bildad, who answers next, treats him not as confessing guilt but as justifying himself, on which very ground the dispute goes on. John Wesley catches the same appeal to mercy: "seeing thou art so gracious to others, why may not I hope for the same favour from thee?"; and if God do not help speedily, it will be too late to show him kindness.

The grammatical-historical witnesses close the chapter on its theology of sin and pardon. Charles Ellicott observes that in Job's belief sin was the origin of all disaster, so that if he were but pardoned his sorrows would pass, a belief our Lord did not discourage when he joined the healing of the paralytic to the assurance of forgiveness (Mark 2:5). Keil and Delitzsch render the whole verse plainly, why not forgive and take away his sin, "for now shall I sleep in the dust, and thou shalt seek me, but I shall not be," leaving the speech suspended between penitence and despair. The witnesses divide over how much guilt Job means to own, a real transgression to be pardoned, as Gill and Henry hear it, or a plea urged "after the manner of men" by one who still holds his innocence, as Clarke maintains; but they agree that the chapter ends with a dying man's face turned, for all his complaint, toward the God who alone can lift the burden before the dust closes over him.
